title: CityFHEPS Hits $1 Billion
plain_title: The city's rental voucher program now costs more than $1 billion
what_they_audited: A Citizens Budget Commission report examining the cost, growth, effect on shelter use and public reporting of New York City's CityFHEPS rental voucher program.
background: The City Fighting Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement (CityFHEPS) rental voucher program launched in October 2018 and consolidated several city rental subsidy programs into one.

findings.plain: The cost of serving current voucher holders has more than doubled in two years.
findings.quote: Serving the 52,000 existing CityFHEPS voucher holders will cost more than $1.1 billion in fiscal year 2025, more than twice the cost in fiscal year 2023.

findings.plain: The following year's budget for the program is far below the current year's cost.
findings.quote: The fiscal year 2026 CityFHEPs budget is just $519 million

findings.plain: Vouchers are cheaper per night than shelter but cost more over five years because they recur while shelter stays are episodic.
findings.quote: By the end of the fifth year, CityFHEPS will cost the City 27 percent more than shelter for the typical single adult and 64 percent more for families.

findings.plain: Across the current caseload, the five-year cost difference runs into the billions.
findings.quote: For the current 52,000 voucher holders, CityFHEPS will cost $1.8 billion more than shelter over five years.

findings.plain: As voucher numbers grew, the shelter population apart from asylum seekers did not fall.
findings.quote: Despite this increase, the number of individuals in shelter, excluding asylum seekers, has held steady.

findings.plain: The city publishes no performance measures for the program, unlike the federal Section 8 vouchers it administers.
findings.quote: the Mayor’s Management Report (MMR) does not include a single indicator on CityFHEPS

findings.plain: CityFHEPS is now the second largest rental voucher program in the country.
findings.quote: With 52,000 active voucher holders, CityFHEPS is the second largest rental housing voucher program in the country

recommendations: Pause and take stock of the cost-effectiveness of CityFHEPS, including how it compares with other policies and whether its effectiveness varies across groups.

Publicly track and report how CityFHEPS is used and how the Department of Social Services administers it, using measures like those the Mayor's Management Report already carries for Section 8 vouchers.
Decide what level of CityFHEPS spending is appropriate and sustainable as part of a broader affordable housing strategy, and target vouchers to the households that will see the most benefit.
